title: The sorrowful mysteries
hookLine: the agony, the scourging, the thorns, the carrying, the cross (Tuesdays and Fridays)
carry: walk the hard road with him

cards: A diagnosis. A funeral. A night in a hospital corridor with bad coffee.
When someone is living through a week like that, there's often nothing anyone can fix. What's left is to stay, and walk next to them for a while.

On Tuesdays and Fridays, Catholics who pray the rosary do something like that with Jesus. They take the beads and walk through the last night and day of his life, one decade at a time. Five scenes, none of them easy.

teach.h: THE GARDEN, THE WHIP, THE THORNS.
teach.b: First, the agony in the garden. The night before he dies, Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and Luke says his sweat fell like drops of blood.

In the Douay-Rheims Bible his prayer is this: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Second, the scourging at the pillar: the Roman soldiers whip him.
Third, the crowning with thorns: they twist a crown out of thorns, throw a purple cloak on him, and mock him as a king.

Fourth, the carrying of the cross, through the streets, with a stranger named Simon of Cyrene pressed into helping. Fifth, the crucifixion: darkness over the land at midday, and death. Notice the word agony.

teach.h: AGONIA: A STRUGGLE, NOT ONLY PAIN.
teach.b: In Luke's Greek it's agonia, a word Greeks also used for the strain of a contest: a struggle, not only pain. Why would anyone choose to pray through this, twice a week? Catholics give a few answers.
One: love stays. Mary stood by the cross, and praying these mysteries is a way of standing there too. Two: the sorrowful mysteries are for people who are suffering.

teach.h: A DECADE FOR SOMEONE WHO HURTS.
teach.b: Someone in chemo, someone grieving, someone in prison can find their own night in his.

teach.h: NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.
teach.b: Some Catholics offer a sorrowful decade for a particular person who is hurting. Three: they don't end here. The rosary never leaves him in the tomb; tomorrow comes the glory.
And one practical note: in his 2002 letter on the rosary, Pope John Paul the Second suggested the sorrowful mysteries for Tuesdays and Fridays, and some also pray them on the Sundays of Lent.

how: Catholics who pray the rosary usually meditate on the sorrowful mysteries on Tuesdays and Fridays, and some through Lent, offering a decade for someone who is suffering.

games.why: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." he asks honestly, and then he hands it over.

practice: In the garden, Jesus asks his friends to stay awake with him, and they fall asleep.
Rest your eyes, open and soft, on one spot, picture the night, the olive trees, the friends asleep, and keep watch; when your mind drifts, come back, the way you'd come back to a friend.
If you pray the rosary, you can pray a sorrowful decade here; if you don't, just keep watch.

wordCard.voice: Sorrowful mysteries. The garden, the pillar, the thorns, the cross carried, the cross. Five hard scenes, walked beside him. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Luke 22:44: struggle, anguish, also the strain of a contest. English agony comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: walk the hard road with him. Sometimes staying is the whole gift. Day one hundred twenty-one, done.
